title: Lawyer
oneLiner: Research and drafting hours are evaporating. The bar card and the blame are not transferable.
summary: Law is protected by two walls that have nothing to do with capability: you must be licensed to practise, and someone must be liable when the advice is wrong. Neither wall stops the work inside from being automated, and the billable-hour engine is where the damage lands. Document review, first-pass research and standard drafting were the profitable base of large firms and the training ground for juniors; both are collapsing at once. Litigation strategy, negotiation, courtroom judgment and the client relationship stay human — but the pyramid that funded them is losing its bottom layer, and firms have not worked out what replaces it.

tasks.name: Document review & discovery
tasks.note: Machine review at a scale and cost no associate team matches. This was a major revenue line; it is now a software licence.

tasks.name: Legal research & memo drafting
tasks.note: First-pass research is minutes, not days. A lawyer still verifies every citation — models still invent cases, and courts still sanction people for it.

tasks.name: Standard contract drafting
tasks.note: Templates plus generation cover routine agreements. The negotiated clauses, the ones that decide who loses, remain argued by people.

tasks.name: Due diligence & compliance review
tasks.note: Flagging is automated and better than manual. Deciding what a flag means for this deal is not.

tasks.name: Litigation strategy & advocacy
tasks.note: Reading a judge, choosing which argument to abandon, deciding when to settle. Adversarial judgment under incomplete information.

tasks.name: Negotiation & client counsel
tasks.note: Clients in legal trouble are frightened. They are buying a person who will sit across from them and say what to do.

tasks.name: Signing, representing, being liable
tasks.note: Unauthorised practice rules and malpractice liability mean a licensed human must own the advice. This is the hardest wall on the site.

whatSurvives: The licence, the courtroom, and the person the client can hold responsible.
adaptPrompt:
You are my legal research and drafting assistant. I am a licensed practitioner. You do not give legal advice; you prepare work product that I verify, own and sign.

I will give you: jurisdiction, area of law, the facts as I have them, and the document or question.

For research tasks:
1. Set out the applicable framework — statute, regulation, leading authorities — and mark clearly where you are uncertain about currency.
2. Give me the strongest version of the argument against my client's position first, then my position. I need the weakness before I need the pitch.
3. Every citation gets flagged UNVERIFIED. I will check each one. Never present a case, section or quote as confirmed.
4. Identify what facts I am missing that would change the analysis.

For drafting tasks:
1. Draft in the register and format of the jurisdiction I named.
2. Mark every clause where a real negotiation choice exists, with the position it favours and the fallback I could accept.
3. List the risks I am accepting on my client's behalf by using this draft as-is.

Absolute rules: never invent authority. If you do not know whether a case exists or is still good law, say exactly that. Never state a conclusion as settled law — frame it as an analysis I will verify. Flag anything that touches privilege, conflicts, or a deadline.
